Left: the colors 0, 1, 2 on the triangle and 0 on C-D never meet twice at a node, so is_valid_edge_coloring() returns True. Right: C-D is recolored to 1, the color of B-C, and the two meet at C (in the accent color), so is_valid_edge_coloring() returns False." width="100%"} The edge counterpart of `is_valid_coloring()`: it checks that, at every node, the colored edges meeting there all have different colors. Use it to check an edge coloring built by hand, loaded from a file or edited after `edge_coloring()`. A few details of the check: - edge direction is ignored, and parallel edges count as sharing both of their nodes - a self-loop meets its node only once, so it conflicts with the node's other edges but not with itself - edges missing from `coloring=` are skipped, so a *partial* coloring is reported as valid when none of its colored edges conflict - keys that are not edge IDs in the graph are ignored ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [coloring]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [dict[int, int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A dictionary mapping edge IDs to colors, such as the output of `edge_coloring()`. Only equality between colors matters. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if no two colored edges that share a node have the same color. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~edge_coloring`) : Find an edge coloring with at most one more color than the maximum degree. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a triangle, all three edges meet in pairs, so they need three different colors: ::: {#ca246e58 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(3) ab, bc, ca = sorted(g.get_edge_ids()) g.is_valid_edge_coloring({ab: 0, bc: 1, ca: 2}), g.is_valid_edge_coloring({ab: 0, bc: 0}) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (True, False) ``` ::: :::
